(p-٢٤٩) Surat ʿAbasa, also called al-Ṣākhkha (The Deafening Blast).

Its purpose is to explain ﴿You are only a warner to those who fear it﴾ [al-Naziʿat: 45]. The greatest aim is the purification of the one who is receptive to fear, through warning about the Resurrection. Its ability to occur has been established by evidence from the beginning of creation from man. This is combined with the two (the beginning and the return) in regard to his food, and with wonder at those who turned away despite the existence of the evidence. It also points out that wealth and luxury are signs of aversion, of unreceptiveness, and of a readiness for disbelief and wickedness, and that calamities are signs of purity, of turning towards Allah, of the humbling of hearts, and of the elevation of souls towards noble goals. Whoever is more firmly rooted in calamities, his heart is softer and more refined, and so he is more fearful, and so turning towards him is more beloved and more fitting. Its name, ʿAbasa, indicates this through reflection on its verses and contemplation of its endings and purposes. Likewise al-Ṣākhkha is the blast that blows away its humans and its sparks, and al-Bākha (the one that shines forth).

(In the name of Allah), who has the far-reaching power and the dazzling wisdom. (The Most Merciful), who has encompassed all with the manifest blessing of existence, then with the radiant signs of clarification. (The Most Compassionate), who has specially favoured His friends by completing His blessing upon them, so that through them they travel on towards His good pleasure.

* *

(p-٢٥٠) Because He, glory be to Him, restricted (the warning) to warning those who fear, and because ʿAbd Allah ibn Umm Maktum, the blind man (may Allah be pleased with him), had come to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he was one of the foremost (in Islam), and at the time of his coming the Prophet (ﷺ) was occupied with calling some of the chieftains of Quraysh to Allah, and he had found from them a kind of softness, ʿAbd Allah (may Allah be pleased with him) began to ask him [while he did not know what he was engaged in, he asked him] to teach him and instruct him [from what Allah had taught him]. So (the Prophet) disliked to cut off his speech with those people, out of fear that he would miss from them what he hoped for, namely their Islam, which would be followed by the Islam of many of their followers. So he turned away from him and faced them, and the dislike appeared on his face. Glory be to Him and exalted, He gently rebuked him for being occupied with those who would not be guided, and for being so intent on one who was not likely to fear (Allah), being captivated by the adornment of the worldly life and devoting himself wholly to what perishes. So He said, clarifying the nobility of poverty, the elevation of its rank, the excellence of the people of religion even if they are humble, and the baseness of the people of this world even if they are adorned, honouring him (ﷺ) through the grammatical style of the third person, as Saʿd ibn Muʿadh (may Allah be pleased with him) said when he judged concerning Banu Qurayza, pointing toward the direction of the Prophet (ﷺ) while turning away from it out of modesty and reverence for him (ﷺ): ﴿He frowned﴾, that is, he did what is the greatest of our creation, and we exalt him from being addressed with such a rebuke to his face, the action of one who dislikes something, the frowning of the face, due to his human nature, when he is prevented from what he wants. It gave notice of praising him (ﷺ) by saying that this was contrary to what He had instilled in him of mercy towards the poor, of love for them, and of joy at their nearness and companionship. (p-٢٥١) [By His saying] ﴿and turned away﴾, that is, he burdened himself with turning away from him, hoping that those nobles he was addressing would accept Islam, so that Islam would be strengthened by them, and their followers would become Muslims through their Islam, so that the word of Allah would be exalted [for the sake of ...]

Surah 80, verse 2:

﴿That the blind man came to him.﴾ He (the Prophet) ought to have been most attentive and generous towards him, to compensate for his disability and to acknowledge his right in coming. He mentioned him by his description (as "the blind man") to indicate his excuse for interrupting the speech and to stir up compassion and mercy towards him. Thereafter, whenever the Prophet (ﷺ) saw him, he would say: "Welcome to the one for whose sake my Lord rebuked me." He also appointed him (Ibn Umm Maktum) as his deputy over the noble city of Madinah during two of his military expeditions. Anas ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "I saw him on the day of al-Qadisiyyah, wearing a coat of mail and carrying a black banner," may Allah be pleased with him.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 80, verse 3:

When he (the Prophet) recognized, through the context of the third-person address, what was intended of honoring (ijlal), and since prolonged turning away necessitates contraction (inqibad), he turned toward him (ﷺ) and said: ﴿And what will make you know?﴾ That is: and what thing would make you knowing of his state, even if you strive for that? For indeed, the innermost thoughts (dhawat al-sudur) are known only to Allah, the Exalted. ﴿Perhaps he﴾ — that is, the blind man — ﴿would purify himself﴾ — that is, he would be in such a condition that his purification and the growth of his good states are hoped for, through what he hears from you, even if only in the least of ways, as indicated by the assimilation of the tā' of the ifti'al form (?), and likewise His saying:

Or he might be reminded, so the reminder benefits him. That is, it may happen that he takes heed of something that becomes a cause of his purification and remembrance, even if that taking heed is at the lowest level that brings him out of disbelief, for good is not belittled in any of its forms. The consequence of his purification and remembrance is His saying: ﴿so the reminder benefits him﴾, that is, immediately after his remembrance, and its cause being ﴿the Reminder﴾. In this there is an indication that his turning away was for the purification and remembrance of others. [The reading of the verb in the accusative (فَتَنْفَعَهُ) is on the basis that it is the answer (جَوَاب) to "لَعَلَّ" (laʿalla, "perhaps").]

When he had mentioned the frowning and the turning away from him, thereby making clear their opposite toward the one who was turning toward them, he clarified that, saying: ﴿As for him who thinks himself self-sufficient﴾, i.e., he who sought wealth (al-ghina), which is property and abundance, and found it, even though he did not fear (God) and did not come to you.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 80, verse 6:

﴿So you attend to him﴾, i.e., rather than the blind man, ﴿you give yourself over to him﴾, by turning toward him with eagerness and striving to admonish him, hoping for his Islam and the Islam of his followers through his own. They were ʿUtbah ibn Rabiʿah, Abu Jahl, and [Ubayy and] Umayyah, the two sons of Khalaf. The omission of the taa' of the tafaʿʿul form (tafaʿʿul, the reflexive verb pattern) in the reading of the majority (qiraʾah, a canonical mode of recitation), and its assimilation in the reading of Nafiʿ and Ibn Kathir, indicate that this was done in a light manner, as is the habit of sensible people.

Al-Imam Abu Jaʿfar Ibn al-Zubayr said: When He, glory be to Him, said ﴿Indeed, in that is a lesson for whoever fears﴾ [al-Naziʿat: 26], and after ﴿You are only a warner for those who fear it﴾ [al-Naziʿat: 45], this other surah opened with an example that reveals the purpose concerning the state of the people of remembrance and fear, and the gracious care of the Lord toward them. [Even if they] are, in their worldly life, obscure and of no account in people's eyes, they are in His presence, glory be to Him, among those whom He has chosen for His worship, for His people, for obedience to Him, and for responding to His Messenger ﷺ, and His esteem for them is exalted. ["Many a dishevelled, dusty person, who is looked down upon, if he swears by Allah, Allah will fulfil his oath."] Among them is Ibn Umm Maktum, the blind muezzin of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, [and he is] the one because of whom the surah was revealed. It came in the manner of reproach, as an admonition to His Prophet ﷺ and an alert that he should train his noble self to be patient with [the likes of] Ibn Umm Maktum, and not belittle them, and far be it from him ﷺ to do so. But the warning against this, even if it had no actual effect, indicates the great care for the one being warned. Among such examples is His saying, glory be to Him, ﴿If you were to associate others with Him, your deeds would surely be lost﴾ [al-Zumar: 65], and ﴿Do not invoke with Allah another god﴾ [al-Qasas: 88], and ﴿Do not walk upon the earth exultantly﴾ [al-Isra': 37]. These are many. Elaborating on this kind does not suit our purpose in this discourse.

When Ibn Umm Maktum entered upon him ﷺ, asking and seeking guidance, the Prophet ﷺ was speaking with a man from the nobles of Quraysh, and he was eager for his Islam, hoping to rescue him from the Fire and to rescue his kin and followers. So this man, because he was hoping for [Islam from him], continued in his demand, and the Prophet ﷺ entrusted Ibn Umm Maktum's [request] to his own [later] belief, and he neglected to answer him promptly, and his persistent urging was difficult for him, out of fear that the Hereafter would slip away and that the man would turn back on his heels and perish. [Then] He, glory be to Him and exalted, reproached him, saying: ﴿He frowned and turned away﴾ [ʿAbasa: 1], ﴿because the blind man came to him﴾ [ʿAbasa: 2], ﴿And what would make you know? Perhaps he might purify himself﴾ [ʿAbasa: 3], ﴿or be reminded, and the reminder would benefit him﴾ [ʿAbasa: 4]. These are, from Him, glory be to Him, binding (commands). It had already been mentioned in this surah, before the words of Moses, peace be upon him: ﴿Would you like to purify yourself?﴾ [al-Naziʿat: 18]. Yet that man was not granted this, nor did he benefit from his widespread fame in his worldly life, nor did what he gained in it avail him. The sources of his planning came to nothing, and the reports became obscure to him, until he said: ﴿I know of no god for you other than myself. So kindle for me, O Haman, [a fire] upon the clay, and make for me a tower that I may look upon the god of Moses﴾ [al-Qasas: 38]. ﴿Indeed, I think he is a liar.﴾ And thus was the evil of his deeds made attractive to Pharaoh, and he was barred from the path [Ghafir: 37]. So how could he purify himself? Had happiness preceded for him, he would have seen, from his own condition, the eye of frivolity and play at the moment of his shameful utterance: ﴿Am I not better than this one who is contemptible?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 52].

As for Ibn Umm Maktum, since the good outcome had preceded for him, the lack of worldly fame did not harm him, nor did his blindness diminish him. Rather, his Lord exalted his station when there was revealed concerning him: ﴿And what would make you know? Perhaps he might purify himself﴾ [ʿAbasa: 3], ﴿or be reminded, and the reminder would benefit him﴾ [ʿAbasa: 4]. How glorious is such a fame, how exalted! This is unlike the one whose mention was put forward, who was driven away, did not purify himself, and did not benefit from the reminder when it was directed at him ﴿You are only a warner for those who fear it﴾ [al-Naziʿat: 45], like Ibn Umm Maktum. And of the same pattern as what was revealed concerning Ibn Umm Maktum is His saying, exalted be He: ﴿And keep yourself patient with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His countenance﴾ [al-Kahf: 28], [and His saying: ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His countenance﴾ [al-Anʿam: 52]]. So blessed is our Lord, how great is His kindness to His servants. O Allah, do not make us despair of Your mercy, do not make us lose hope in Your kindness, and do not cut us off from You by Your bounty and Your beneficence. [End.]

When his doing that was the act of one who fears that blame might fall on him for their remaining in disbelief, He showed him that he was free of that, saying: ﴿And what﴾ [i.e., what did you do? - ] it is upon you, while the situation is that there is nothing upon you, i.e., no blame, in ﴿that he does not purify himself﴾ at all, not even with the slightest purification - indicated by the idgham (assimilation) - ﴿Upon you is only the conveying (of the message)﴾. It is also permissible for this to be an interrogative, i.e., "And what would be upon you in his not purifying himself?" and in it there is an indication that one must strive hard in purifying the follower whom one knows to be receptive.

When he mentioned the one who considers himself self-sufficient, He mentioned its opposite, saying: ﴿But as for him who came to you﴾ while ﴿hastening﴾, that is, hurrying, out of eagerness for what you possess of good that reminds one of God, and he is poor.

Here is the translation:

﴿And he﴾, that is, while the state is that he ﴿fears﴾, that is, there exists fear of God Most High, and of the disbelievers in their harm, in coming to the Prophet ﷺ, and of the obstacles of the road because of his blindness.

﴿So you, from him,﴾ meaning: specifically in that gathering, given that it was the situation in the outcome, ﴿were distracted﴾, meaning you were occupied on account of those nobles (p-٢٥٦) whom you wished to bring to Islam, because of their influence in spreading the religion, a light preoccupation, as indicated by the deletion of the ta' in ﴿تلهى﴾. It comes from lahha 'anhu, like radiya, meaning: when one diverted himself, became heedless, and abandoned. In this expression there is an indication that preoccupation with those nobles has no benefit, as the morphological forms of the root (tasarif al-madda) convey, and that whoever seeks a person and pushes through the necks of people to reach him has a great right over you. The verse is an example of ihtibak (a rhetorical device in which each of two complementary elements is left implicit and understood from the other): the mention of wealth first indicates poverty second, and the mention of coming and lowliness second indicates their opposites first. The secret of this warning is to guard against what human nature inclines to: the tendency toward the wealthy, and the disregard for the right of the one who comes, in order to magnify the very act of his coming.

When the reproach, which is part of the manner of loved ones, was hinting at the prohibition of turning away from the one against whom the reproach was directed, and against everyone whose condition is like his, and of being preoccupied away from one who is eager, He stated it explicitly, saying: ﴿By no means!﴾ That is, do not do that at all. The matter of decree and destiny is not as the servants suppose, nor does it proceed according to the causes you know. Rather, it lies beyond their knowledge, following a judgment that is too subtle for their thoughts and understandings. Then He gave the reason for that, emphasizing it in refutation of their denial, saying:

﴿Indeed, it﴾, that is, the Qur'an. Perhaps He made the pronoun feminine in view of the verses or chapters recited to them in that gathering. ﴿is a reminder﴾, that is, it reminds them with a great reminder, by which, if they reflect upon it, they will witness it within themselves (p-257) and in the horizons. There is nothing in it except that they would recognize it if they turned to it with their whole being. So there is no obligation upon the one who reminds with it except conveying (the message). Whoever turns to it, then welcome and ease; and whoever turns away, then distance [for him] and destruction.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 80, verse 12:

Since He, glorified is He, had created for man intellect (ʿaql) and free choice (ikhtiyār), and had made easy the matter of the Qur'an in memorization and understanding for whoever turns to it, He made the following statement a consequence of that: ﴿Whoever wills﴾, that is, remembers it after the will of God Most High, as its restriction has been stated in the Qur'an more than once, ﴿remembers it﴾, that is, memorizes the whole Qur'an and recalls what it contains of admonition without repetition and without a treatment that would necessitate turning away from some of those who come forward eager to learn. And to indicate that he memorizes all of it, He used the pronoun (ḍamīr) ﴿it﴾ in the singular.

In the commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 80, verse 13:

Since the sense is: while the Qur'an is affirmed (muthbitan), or while the one who remembers it is affirming it (muthbitan) [...], He said, describing the reminder (tadhkirah) and making clear its nobility by ennobling its container and the container of its container: ﴿in scrolls﴾, that is, things in which it is written, of paper and other materials, ﴿exalted﴾, that is, repeatedly honored, and held in high esteem in the heavens and the earth, in every nation and every religious community [...].

[Qur'an 80:14] "Exalted (marfu'ah)" means: its worth is established by the elevation of everyone, especially of the One to whom all command belongs. "Purified (mutahharah)" means: it is free from the hands of the lowly folk and from their saying that it is poetry, or sorcery, or the like.

Also, the word "in" (fi) is linked here to "recorded" (muthbat), with the fatha or kasra reading, according to the difference between the two meanings. His statement, explaining the nobility of that container for that content, points to the utmost nobility of what is contained.

﴿With the hands of scribes﴾, that is, scribes who make manifest the writing with what it contains of wondrous reports and lofty rulings in [every -] circumstance. If what the preposition is attached to is with a fatha (سَفَرَة, *safara*), then it is literal, in that they are angels who copy it from the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), or it is the plural of *sāfir* (سافِر), either in the sense of the writers (الكِتاب), or of the traveller (المُسافِر), that is, one who covers the distance, or of the envoy (السَّفِير), who is the reconciler, because they are envoys between God and His prophets, and through them the affair of religion and the world is set right. If it is with a kasra (سِفْر, *sifr*), then it is metaphorical, because whoever devotes himself to writing down the Remembrance becomes refined, in the present or in the ultimate outcome, generally. And the root (تَرْكِيب) *s-f-r* signifies unveiling (لِلْكَشْف).

[Kiraam] meaning: they embody noble character traits, even though they are honored by God. [Barararah] meaning: they are pious, at the highest levels of piety and generosity, and the most esteemed and far-reaching of them.

When the description of the scribes, whose hands are a receptacle for the pages, which are themselves a receptacle for the Reminder, was given these lofty attributes, this was to alert to the exaltedness of what is written, the greatness of its rank, the magnitude of its effects, and the manifestation of all this to whoever reflects upon it, contemplates it with due contemplation, and examines it closely (p-259). He followed it [with His saying], denouncing those who [do not] turn wholeheartedly to it, and invoking against them with the greatest of the world's hardships, which is killing, in the form of a report because it is more eloquent: ﴿Man is killed﴾. That is, this species, intimate with itself, forgetful of its Lord, arrogant toward others, and self-admiring for the qualities its Creator originated for it, has been killed by His curse and expulsion, and it is finished with the easiest and least effort from everyone for whom that is valid, because it is the swiftest thing toward corruption, since it is built upon deficiencies, except those whom God protects. ﴿How disbelieving he is!﴾ That is, how intense is his concealment of the truth, his denial of it, and his obstinacy regarding it, in denying the Resurrection, associating others with his Lord, and other such matters. So it is a supplication against him with the most odious supplication, and an expression of wonder at his excess in concealing the excellences of the Qur'an, which are not hidden from anyone, and its proofs of the Hour, and everything that does not allow anyone to find fault with any of them. This supplication, despite its brevity, indicates great wrath and eloquent censure. Although it concerns a particular person, the lesson lies in its generality for everyone who denies God's blessing. It is narrated that it was revealed concerning Utbah ibn Abi Lahab, who was angry with his father, then embraced Islam. Then his father sought to reconcile him, gave him wealth, and equipped him to go to Syria. He sent word to the Prophet (ﷺ) that he disbelieves in the Lord of the star when it sets, and he spoke obscenely about other matters. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O God, send upon him one of Your dogs." When he reached a place on the road where there was a lion (p-260), he mentioned the supplication. He offered those with him a thousand dinars if he survived the morning, so they placed him in the middle of the caravan, among the goods and the baggage. The lion came to the baggage, leapt, and there it was upon him, and it tore him apart. His father would lament him and weep over him, and he said: "Muhammad never said anything except that it came to pass." Despite that, what he knew of this did not benefit him. Glory be to Him in whose hand are the hearts; He misguides whom He wills and guides whom He wills, and all of that, from His guidance and His misguidance, bears witness that to Him belongs all praise.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 80, verse 18:

Since the greatest part of the wonder-inducing address (al-ta'ajjub) directed at him (the disbeliever) was concerned with his denial of the Hour (al-sa'ah), because its proofs are extremely manifest in the Qur'an, and because in these surahs the establishment of proofs for it has continued to the point where nothing more can be added, he began to establish the proof for it through the sign within the souls (ayat al-anfus), from the beginning of creation, in a style that makes clear how base and contemptible (man's origin) is, and that the One who clothed him in the garments of honor after that baseness and contemptibility is deserving of his gratitude, not his disbelief. So He said, alerting him by means of a question: ﴿From what thing﴾, and the interrogation is for affirmation together with belittlement, ﴿did He create him?﴾

Then He answered, signaling that the answer is clear and needs no pause at all. So He said, showing its insignificance: ﴿From a drop of seminal fluid﴾, i.e., from very little water and from nothing else, ﴿He created him﴾, i.e., brought him into existence, determined in the form of shaping that he has, ﴿then He proportioned him﴾, i.e., prepared him for what is fitting of the outward and inward limbs, the forms and the stages (p-261) until he became fit for that. Then He made his passage through three darknesses: the darkness of the belly, then of the womb, then of the placenta. Or, according to what the people of anatomy (tashrih) have said, they are three membranes: the first is the placenta, which is connected to the navel of the fetus and supplies it with nourishment; the second receives its urine; and the third receives the vapors that rise from it, like the sweat and filth in the bodies of adults. And He gave him the power for what He willed [from him].

**﴿Then﴾** means after the term has ended. **﴿the way﴾** means the most complete in generality, breadth, and clarity, and no other. It is his exit from his mother's womb, and his path toward Paradise or the Fire. **﴿He made it easy﴾** means He made his matter easy in his exit, by opening the mouth of the womb and inspiring him to turn around (in the womb). He made the path of good and evil easy for him [ ] and gave him an intellect that guides him toward what has been made easy for him of both. In this there is an allusion that this world is a place of passage, and the goal is other than it, namely the Hereafter, to which this world points. For this reason He followed it with His words, counting death among the blessings. If a person remained alive, with what reaches him of weakness and fear, he would be in the utmost ugliness and a source of gloating for his enemies and of distress for his allies. Moreover, death is the cause of eternal life.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 80, verse 21:

﴿Then﴾, that is, after matters which He, glory be to Him, ordained for him as to his term and the changes of his state (p-262) ﴿He caused him to die﴾. He indicated the obligation of hastening to the preparation of the burial by the particle fa' of immediate sequence in His saying ﴿then He buried him﴾, meaning He made for him a grave and concealed him in it, and commanded his burial as an honour to him and as protection from wild beasts. Iqbar (burial) is your making a grave for the dead person and your handing over the slain to his family so that they may bury him. The meaning is a reminder of favour: that He made for mankind a place suitable for their burial, and made it after death such that one can be enabled to bury him. Had He willed, He would have made him crumble along with the stench and the like that prevents approaching him, or made him such that he is held in contempt and is not buried, like the remaining animals. Thus it is known from this that the beginning of man is a fetid drop, and his end is a foul carcass, and in between he carries filth. So it was none but He who originated him and formed him who honoured him with knowledge, and that is a reason for him to give thanks, not to disbelieve.

Since the duration of the barzakh (the intermediate state between death and resurrection) is long, and the resurrection is a certainty whose time is not known by sight but only by Him, may He be exalted, He expressed the three meanings with the particles of delay and certainty, saying: ﴿Then, when He wills﴾, that is, its raising, ﴿He raises him﴾, that is, He resurrects him from his grave as he was in his worldly life, with the addition that he is upon a strong composition in which the separation of the soul from the body cannot occur.

Since his report that He is with the One who made the way easy for him might lead one to understand that he does not act except in what pleases Him, He negated that by way of deterrence, saying: ﴿Kalla﴾ (No!), that is, so that this human being may desist, the one who knows that these are his states at first, at last, in between, and in his exit, sometimes from the exit of urine and another time from the exit of menstruation, and in his burial place, and so that he may be restrained, and so that he may know himself by abasement, lowliness, need and weakness, and so that he may know his Lord, glorified is He, by might, greatness, majesty, self-sufficiency (al-fana') and the power to honor the lowly and to humble the noble. And [he should know] that He, glorified is He, is not bound by anything, so it does not follow from His making this human being know the way and distinguishing it for him that He is obligated to do so, for He does only what He is not blamed for. Whatever comes from the human being and others is only what He wills: at times He wills their guidance, and at times He wills their misguidance. He may command what He does not will, and will what He does not command nor approve. For this reason He said, as a resumption negating what His facilitating the way had suggested, namely that the human being does everything God commanded him through Him who made the way easy for him: ﴿Lamma yaqdi﴾ (He has not yet fulfilled), that is, the human being has not performed an act that is executed and completed (nafidhan madiyan) ﴿ma amarahu﴾ (what He commanded him), that is, what God commanded him, all of it, without any shortfall. Not from the time he was made responsible until the time he is buried, but from the time Adam, peace be upon him, was brought into existence until the revelation of this verse and until the end of time. This is because the human being is founded upon deficiency, while God is exalted in the most perfect exaltation, and "they did not measure God with His true measure." Also, the human being, who is the species, has not, in its entirety, acted in such a way that not a single individual deviated from doing all that He commanded. Rather, most of the kind has disobeyed Him and denied the Hour, which is the wisdom of existence. And if some of them affirm it, their affirmation of it is a denial, because they believe in things concerning it that are contrary to what it actually is.

(p-264) When He had rebuked him, after detailing [what is his] in himself of signs, and pointed to what he has of deficiencies, He began to establish the proof of his shortcoming, namely that he is not able to thank the Bestower for the blessing in the food by which he is sustained, let alone for other things, in a style indicative of dispersal, by the signs of the horizons, drawing attention to all the other blessings during the period of his remaining alive, which entails the continued need for his Lord. So He said, as a consequence of that: ﴿So let man look⦆ that is, let him direct complete attention to everything he is able to look at with his sight and his insight, and He extended the scope for him, so He said: ﴿at his food﴾, meaning what he eats and what is connected with it, turning to it wholly with consideration of the lessons in it, among them that if We did not make it easy for him, he would perish.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 80, verse 25:

When the intended purpose was to look upon the works of God Most High therein, and the deeds and sayings of man in denying the Resurrection were the deeds of one who denies that work, the Exalted said, detailing what is shared in His special and general knowledge of His works concerning food, emphasizing as an alert that denial of the Resurrection necessitates denial of the originating of plants and their return, and that in an expressive style showing that man is in need of everything that exists, and if anything were lacking from it his affairs would be disordered. He began first with the heavenly, because it is more noble, and with the water which is the life of every thing, as an alert to him regarding the beginning of his creation: ﴿That We⁠﴾, i.e., by virtue of the greatness that is ours, ﴿poured down the water⁠﴾, i.e., that from which We made (p-265) every living thing, ﴿in abundant pouring⁠﴾. Then He mentioned the earth, which in relation to the heaven is like the female in relation to the male, saying:

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 80, verse 26:

﴿Then﴾ i.e., after an interval from the sending down of water, and We varied between them in lands and vegetation, ﴿We split﴾ i.e., by what We possess of majesty, ﴿the earth﴾ with vegetation, which is in the utmost weakness, splitting the hardest of things. How much more so the dry earth, which is greatly cracked when it mixes with water. And he confirmed the meaning, saying: ﴿a splitting﴾.

Then He made the splitting the cause of what serves as an explanation of it, clarifying the need for vegetation by His saying: ﴿So We caused to grow﴾, that is, We made to emerge, upon the aspect of connection that necessitates nourishment and growth, ﴿therein﴾ by means of the splitting, ﴿grain﴾, that is, for the sustenance of humans and other animals, such as wheat, barley, rice, and others.

When the grain was a staple food, he began with it, because it is the foundation of sustenance. He then followed it with what is both fruit and staple: ﴿and grapes﴾, which is fruit in its natural state as grapes, and a staple when it is made into raisins (zabib), dibs (grape molasses), and vinegar (khall). Since this was part of showing the wonders of God's craftsmanship, so as to indicate the power over all things, and thus the power over resurrection, he mentioned what, if taken from its place of growth before it matured, spoils, but if left to ripen becomes firm and fit for storage. He followed it with what spoils if left on its root, but if harvested and treated, becomes fit for storage. Then he followed it with what is not fit for storage in any way: ﴿and fresh herbs﴾, which is the green part of herbs and other plants. It surpasses the two previous items in that it contains both a beneficial medicine and a deadly poison, and in that it is cut again and again and regrows. It is named by the verbal noun qadb, meaning to cut it by mowing or uprooting.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 80, verse 29:

When he had mentioned what is not fit to be eaten except fresh and without delay, he followed it with what does not spoil in any state, neither on its parent tree nor after being picked [and it is fit after being picked], so it is eaten or pressed, and thus it yields oil for lighting, for anointing and for seasoning, and in it is strengthening for the bones and the sinews, and water does not spoil it in any way, just as grapes are pressed so that from them come grape-syrup (dibs), vinegar and other things, whereas once water mixes with it, it spoils. [So he said]: ﴿And olives﴾. Along with what has passed, it has a pungency and a freshness, and in it is the correction of temperament (islah al-mizaj).

When he had mentioned what does not spoil and whose tree endures the cold, he followed it with what is like the grape, eaten on its parent tree and also cut and stored, so it combines sweetness and sourness through vinegar, fruit-eating, strengthening and healing for the deadly poison and the prostrating magic, from the ajwa of the noble city of Madina and other than that, of fruit and tree. Its tree does not endure the cold, so he said: ﴿And palm trees﴾. Each of these trees differs from the others in form, bearing and other respects, while agreeing in soil and irrigation.

(p-267) When He had mentioned these things, the foodstuffs and fruits, for the abundance of their benefits, and gardens gather them and other things along with what they have of the delight of the eye, the joy of the soul, the expansion of the heart, and the opening of the breast, He said: ﴿And gardens﴾, the plural of ḥadīqah (garden), which is a meadow possessing palm trees and trees, or everything enclosed by a wall [building], and it gathers all of that [entirely]. ﴿Dense﴾, the plural of ghalbā' (with a fatḥah on the ghayn and a long vowel), which is a garden with many large, thick, tall trees whose branches are intertwined and densely packed [crowded], a metaphor borrowed from the description of necks. It is said: "Fulān ghalaba," like faraḥa, meaning his neck became thick. Ghalbā' also refers to strong, unyielding tribes, and to elevated hills.

Having mentioned what is enjoyed and stored, He gathered them together and said: ﴿And fruit﴾, meaning fresh fruit by which one enjoys oneself, such as peaches (al-khawkh), grapes (al-'inab), figs (al-tin), apples (al-tuffah), pears (al-kummithra), and plums (al-burquq), of what can be preserved when it is dried and of what cannot. Having mentioned the fruit of humans, He mentioned the fruit of the rest of the animals and said: ﴿And grass﴾, meaning pasture, herbage, plants, green vegetation, and fodder, as long as it is green, which is sought out; from abba al-shay', meaning when one aims at it (ab, ya'ubbu, aims for something).

(p-268) When he had gathered what is eaten as food and what is enjoyed as fruit, thereby clearly indicating the completeness of power, he mentioned the blessing in it, striking the heart with the style of direct address, to generalize the individuals after the context of reproach. This is to make explicit that all of them are unable to fulfil gratitude, so how much more so when disbelief is added to that. So he said: ﴿as a provision﴾, and it is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl). When he had mentioned what people eat and what is fed to animals, and the context here concerned human food, he put their pronoun first, saying: ﴿for you and your livestock﴾, unlike what is in al-Sajda, as has passed. The livestock are, through them, the complete benefit for the human being, through the blessings they provide in riding, eating, drinking, clothing, adornment and all other benefits. He mentioned this clearly, alluding to the metals (al-ma'ādin), because some of what has passed cannot be completed without them, namely the tools of planting, harvesting, cooking, kneading and other things, and the angels who manage what God has directed them to in all of that. This indicates that all existence was created for the sake of human benefits, so that he may give thanks, not that he may disbelieve. Power has also demonstrated this with certainty, and so it demonstrates the power to resurrect.

When he had mentioned the wondrous workmanship in food, and that it is harvested and then returns, especially pasture, which the autumn reaches so that it dries out, then is shattered by the winds and scattered over the earth, then becomes dust, and then God sends the rain, which gathers it from the earth after it has become dust, and then makes it grow again as it was, and that this is the same as bringing the dead to life, the truth of what preceded about resurrection after burial was confirmed. This [discussion] also reminded [us] of the matter of our father Adam, peace be upon him, when God commanded him to eat from the Garden except from the tree that He forbade him. When he ate from it, He expelled him from the Garden and confined him to a dwelling that is neither a garden nor a fire, nor anything else, but is a mixture of the two abodes and like a barzakh (intermediate realm) between them. In it are things that remind of this and things that remind of that, and in it are examples of all existing things. He said, explaining the cause of what established the bringing to life for the resurrection to the gathering place, expressing it with the particle of certainty, because the Hour is something that must come and from which there is no escape, since it is the secret of the universe. In it is the reckoning of those who were made successors in this existence, upon whom the blessings that He deposited in it were poured out, and He indicated that they are unable to render thanks for them, and that many of them, indeed most of them, added to that by denying them. This necessarily requires their reckoning for what they did with what they were made successors over and entrusted with, as is the custom of every one entrusted and made successor: ﴿Then when the Shriekingly Loud Blast comes﴾, meaning, when it occurs and is found, because everything that is to happen is as if it has met you and come to you [-]. ﴿The Shriekingly Loud Blast﴾, meaning the great cry by which hearing is greatly sounded, to the point that it nearly deafens [the ears] because of its intensity, as if it pierces them because of the force of its impact and the greatness of its thunder, and the ears are compelled to incline toward it [i.e. - ] to listen. It is one of the names of the Resurrection. The root of ṣakk is striking a solid object against a solid, smooth surface.

(p-270) Since describing it by what happens in it is more awe-inspiring, He said, substituting for "idhā" (when) what indicates its response, of the sort: "each one is occupied with himself, and has no leisure for anyone else": ﴿On the Day a man flees﴾, i.e., the one who is the greatest of creation in manliness. And since the context concerns fleeing, He began with the lowest in rank in terms of affection and protection, and then ascended through them, and delayed the most obligatory in that, so the most obligatory came last. This is unlike what is in "sa'ala" (asked), as has passed, so He said: ﴿from his brother﴾, because he familiarizes with him in childhood, and may rely upon him in adulthood, along with the long companionship and the intensity of closeness in kinship, so he is held in the utmost honor by him.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 80, verse 35:

Since the mother shares with him in intimacy (al-ilf), and the obligation to protect her is greater than that owed to a brother, for she is more intimate to him, more tender toward her, and more compassionate and gentle toward her, He said ﴿and his mother﴾. And since the father is greater than her in intimacy, because he is closer in kind (al-nawʿ), and the child's affection toward him is stronger, owing to the greater benefit he brings, more than to those before him, He said: ﴿and his father﴾.

Now when the wife, who is fit to be a companion, is closest to the heart and most deeply rooted in affection, and a person is most protective of her in times of hardship, He said: ﴿and his companion﴾. Perhaps He made it singular to indicate that she holds the highest rank of affection in his heart, such that he does not become intimate with anyone other than her.

And since a father has, toward his children, a love and tenderness, and a sharing of secrets and consultation in affairs, that no one else has, and for this reason his provision and his life are lost without them, He said: ﴿and his sons﴾. Although there is included among them the small one, for whom he is most compassionate, and the grown one, who is greater in his heart and more noble in his eyes, and those between them, both male and female.

Having mentioned his flight, which his own affairs prevented him from undertaking in comfort, he gave the reason, saying: ﴿For every man among them, that Day, will be a matter that suffices him﴾. That is, even if he was the greatest of people in manliness (muruwwah). ﴿That Day﴾, meaning [when] these great calamities, severe hardships and pains will occur. ﴿A matter﴾, meaning a grave, momentous affair. ﴿That suffices him﴾, meaning it is enough for him in terms of concern, to the extent that it leaves him no share that he could direct toward anyone else, and it compels him to remain fixed on the matter, namely his own abode, which occupies him; and although he knows that they will follow him and fears that they will demand from him, because of the distress they are in, what he may have fallen short of regarding their rights.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 80, verse 38:

When He mentioned the Day, He divided its people into the two categories that were intended by the reminder at the beginning of the surah. So He said, indicating the inner states by the most noble of outward signs: ﴿Faces that Day will be bright﴾, meaning: since what came before of fleeing and other things [has occurred], ﴿shining﴾, meaning white and radiant with brightness and luminosity, from asfara al-subh (the dawn lit up), when it brightens and becomes luminous.

Laughing, joyful, for what it knows of its happiness; ﴿mustabshirah﴾, that is, seeking to have its complexion change, which is the change of the skin from joy, and bringing that about. It is radiant and bright, because of what it sees of the good tidings of the angels. This is in contrast to what it used to be in the world: the frowning and changing of faces and their paleness from fear of God Most High, and from what appears of His majesty at the Hour, such as Ibn Umm Maktum, may Allah be pleased with him, whom the fear of the Hour moved to carry the banner in the most severe battles, such as the Day of al-Qadisiyyah, and to stand firm with it until he became like a pillar that does not move from its place at all, in order to please the Worshipped One.

When the people of happiness were mentioned, those who turn toward goodness and are afflicted in themselves with what expiates their misdeeds and raises their ranks, he mentioned their opposites, and said, may He be exalted: ﴿And faces﴾. He emphasized by repeating the adverbial phrase to remove doubt, and said: ﴿on that day﴾ [i.e., when what was mentioned occurs], ﴿upon them﴾, i.e., clinging to them with dominance and elevation, ﴿will be dust-darkness﴾, i.e., dark dust-coloring, as if it had reached a state where it seems dust has risen over them. They are ﴿frowning﴾, fearful, terrified, startled, and that is because of the hardships that befall them, the great crowding, the terror of the heart, and the remembrance of the severe distresses to which they are heading.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 80, verse 41:

﴿Tarhaquha﴾ means: it covers it, overpowers it, and overtakes it. ﴿Qatarah﴾ means: like dust, blackness, and darkness, the opposite of brightness (al-Isfar). So they are weeping and frowning, because of what they used to be in the world (p-273) of joy, play, laughter, and feeling safe from punishment. The verse is of the type called al-Ihtibak (a rhetorical device in which each of two opposites is mentioned while its counterpart is omitted, and the omitted one is understood from the mentioned one): mentioning brightness and gladness first indicates fear and terror second, and mentioning dust second indicates whiteness and light first. The secret of this is that He mentioned the sign of ease and the sign of hardship, because both are evident, as encouragement and warning.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 80, verse 42:

When this matter was terrifying, and the wicked person, because of the rust (rayn) upon his heart and the hardness (qasawa) in it, has little fear of the appointed term and no thought for what tomorrow may bring, due to the two desires that have overcome him, the beast-like (sab'iyya) and the animal (bahimiyya) desires, unlike the God-fearing person in all of that, he resumed the report, increasing the terror, and said: ﴿Those﴾, that is, the distant and the hateful, ﴿they are﴾, that is, exclusively and no others, ﴿the disbelievers﴾, that is, those who concealed the signs of faith, ﴿the wicked﴾, that is, those who went out of the circle of the Law in a grievous manner, to the extent that they were deeply immersed in that disbelief and wickedness. They are, for the most part, the affluent (mutrafun), whose wealth carries them to arrogance, insolence and exultation. Because they combined disbelief and wickedness, He combined for them dust (ghabara) and darkness (qatara), just as there appears on the faces of the Ethiopians (zunuj) from the blackness (biqa'a) when dust and filth cover their faces. Thus the last of it has returned upon the first, regarding who deserves to be turned away from and who deserves to be turned toward. And God is the Guide.
